title: Drywater now has SOUNDS!
author: DetectiveWorking5512
selftext:
After previously clearing the 2D to 3D conversion, I went back to my previous SFX work to finally add sounds to Drywater. v2.1.1 is now released on the Play Store with a full suite of 150 sfx, along with a couple of smaller bugfixes. The video above is a short example.

[https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.drywater.game](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.drywater.game)

I started the audio work with Claude around a month ago, and gave up because the animal sounds were very frustrating. Picked back up with Gemini via Antigravity, and then switched between the two to finish it off and get them wired into the game.

I also had Claude add a "Sounds" section to my offline toolset (Drywater Workshop) so that I can replace any sound, remix it, adjust the levels, etc, without having to use either Claude or Gemini in the future.

To provide more details, I asked Claude to write up how the process actually went.

BELOW IS AI-WRITTEN:

Until this update, the game had literally zero audio. Now it's shipping with **150 distinct sound effects (257** `.ogg` **files, \~6.1 MB in the APK)** covering footsteps, harvesting, crafting stations, weapons, wildlife, four tameable mount species, biome ambience, and UI.

What made this interesting is that the library was split right down the middle between two AI workflows: **Claude Code** built the pipeline and locked the first **75 sounds**, and then I handed the remaining **75 sounds** (plus a full mix audit) to **Antigravity / Gemini**.

Here's why I switched, what tools and methods actually got it across the finish line, and the lessons I wish I'd known on day one.

# Where Claude Started (and Where It Hit a Wall)

Claude built a local, zero-API Python pipeline (`tools/gen_sfx.py`) driven by a single JSON manifest (`sfx_manifest.json`):

* **Generator:** Local **Stable Audio 3 Small SFX** on CPU (free, \~7–10s per 4s clip after model load).
* **"Slice, don't regenerate":** One 4-second generation holds \~4 strikes, so the script runs envelope-based onset detection to slice variants out of a single take, then normalizes them to **-18 LUFS** (`pyloudnorm`) with a **-1 dBFS** true-peak ceiling.
* **Spectral cleanup:** Every Stable Audio clip had a faint, steady **13–21 kHz whine** ("background hum"), so Claude added an 80 Hz high-pass, 11 kHz low-pass, and `noisereduce` pass.

That worked surprisingly well for the first **75 sounds**—harvesting impacts, footsteps across 7 surfaces, building placement, UI, crafting stations, and weapons. (Human voices failed repeatedly, which accidentally led to one of my favorite design choices: outlaw alerts and townsfolk greetings became plucked banjo riffs instead.)

**Then we hit Mounts and Wildlife** (Horse, Elk, Bear, Cougar — 52 sounds across idle, alert, taming cues, spooks, charges, flees, and deaths — plus 11 ambient critters and biome beds).

Two things broke down at once:

1. **Text-to-audio fell apart on realistic animals.** Text-only horse takes weren't even usable as audition candidates.
2. **Claude is deaf.** It can inspect RMS/LUFS stats and waveforms, but it can't actually listen to an audio file. Every generated take and every candidate recording had to go through my ears first, turning wildlife sourcing into a brutal manual bottleneck.

# How Gemini / Antigravity Finished the Other 75 Sounds

The unlock wasn't "better prompting"—it was **multimodal audio listening** paired with a **hybrid pipeline**. Because Antigravity/Gemini can listen directly to `.wav` files, it could pre-audition raw recordings, generated foley, and composite mixes *by ear* before handing me a shortlist to sign off on.

Of the **75 sounds** it finished, the final breakdown ended up being:

* **36 curated recordings** — strictly commercial-clean sources: Freesound CC0, Sonniss GDC royalty-free bundles, Wikimedia CC0, and **U.S. National Park Service Public Domain** recordings (real Yellowstone grizzly jaw pops and bull elk bugles).
* **22 local AI generations** — mostly Stable Audio 3 `small-sfx` for foley/percussion (hooves, paw pads, seamless gallop loops, saddle creaks, grouse wing-flushes, brush scurries, silver coins, iron vault latch), 2 takes on `medium` (1.4B) for warm equine/elk nostril breaths, and 2 audio-to-audio (`init_audio`) horse whinnies.
* **17 scripted multi-layer composites** — marrying real animal recordings with generated foley inside the pipeline. For example:
   * **Bear charge:** CC0 grizzly triple-roar layered over a generated heavy-lope footstep track ramping gain `0.35 → 1.0`.
   * **Bear alert:** CC0 alarm woof + NPS Yellowstone grizzly jaw pops.
   * **Horse flee:** Audio-to-audio whinny + receding generated dirt gallop.
   * **Mount deaths:** Falling animal groan timed into a heavy packed-dirt body collapse.
   * **Whistler (messenger bird):** CC0 small-bird wing flutter landing into a CC0 white-crowned sparrow chirp.

# Pipeline Upgrades Needed to Make That Work

We extended `gen_sfx.py` so the entire library stayed 100% reproducible from the manifest (zero manual DAW exports):

* **Composite layer engine (**`source: "composite"`**):** Mixes arbitrary `"recording"` and `"gen"` layers with per-layer `offset_s`, `gain`, linear gain ramps (`ramp_start_gain` / `ramp_end_gain`), trims, and fades.
* **Lazy model loading +** `--offline` **flag:** Stopped wasting 15–25 seconds loading PyTorch weights when rebuilding recording-only sounds.
* **Pipeline order bugfix:** Moved tape-style `pitch_semitones` resampling to run *after* filtering and noise profiling—previously, resampling first silently shifted the `[start, end]` timestamps used to sample background noise.
* **Swapped OGG export to** `ffmpeg` **(**`libvorbis -q:a 5`**):** `soundfile`/`libsndfile` on Windows hit a hard `STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW (0xC00000FD)` whenever exporting stereo float64 ambient loops longer than 10 seconds.

Before exporting, Antigravity also ran a **full ear-audit of all 75 of Claude's earlier sounds** (163 files). **70/75 held up**, and **5 got upgraded** (a cleaner death groan, bow nock, seamless forge loop, wooden chest creak distinct from the iron vault, and dropping a clipped 0.28s UI panel variant).

# Bonus: The Two-AI Mix Pass After Wiring

Once all 257 `.ogg` files were wired into Godot (`AudioManager` autoload, 3D voice pool, bus layout, and a limiter on Master), we still had the same problem: **Claude couldn't hear the game mix, and Gemini couldn't play the game.**

So Claude built an automated headless **Listening Reel** in Godot: a debug scenario that freezes the world, plays every single variant of all 150+ sound IDs through the real mixer into 11 section WAVs (plus a 70-second gameplay tour and a 10-minute soak capture), and generates a timestamped Markdown index with peak/RMS stats.

Antigravity then listened through the entire reel + tour + soak like a sound engineer:

* Confirmed the Master limiter (`-1 dBFS` ceiling / `-2 dBFS` threshold) only caught 6 brief 0.25s transient peaks across 11+ minutes with zero pumping.
* Confirmed smooth Valley ↔ Town and biome crossfades with no dead-air dips.
* Caught **12 mix issues** that numbers alone missed—like night crickets and winter wind sitting 7–10 dB too hot after I pulled daytime beds down, mountain/snow footsteps disappearing under wind, a marmot whistle and distant elk bugle that were too shy for phone speakers, a stationary `portal_hum` that would drone while crafting, and a chest lid slamming louder than it opened.

All 12 retunes went through our CLI data tool, the reel rebuilt cleanly, and then I sideloaded the APK to my Galaxy S25 for the final call.

# 5 Key Learnings

1. **Use generative audio for foley and textures, not pitched wildlife vocals.** Stable Audio 3 crushed impacts, hooves, gallop loops, saddle leather, and scurry/brush textures—especially once we learned `cfg > 1.0` over-drives `small-sfx` into static and durations under 2s collapse into buzz. For pitched animal calls, commercial-clean recordings + scripted composites beat pure generation every time.
2. **Never pitch-shift small domestic pets down to fake big predators.** Trying to turn housecat hisses and yowls into a cougar by pitching `-3` to `-5.5` semitones via tape resampling stretched the attack formants into cartoon/sci-fi monsters. Un-pitched (or `±0.8 st`) real wildcat recordings (Caracal, studio big-cat) sounded genuinely tense. Steady purrs were the only exception that tolerated `-3.5 st`.
3. **Never trust a Freesound filename or RMS meter—listen to the exact slice.** Direct ear-auditioning caught things metadata never shows: spoken studio slates (`"45"` right before a big-cat roar), zoo crowd/kid chatter hiding in a clip's tail, and a file literally named `Bobcat.wav` that turned out to be a **construction skid-steer loader**.
4. **Noise reduction is a scalpel, not a blanket.** Blanket noise reduction turns broadband textures (snow crunch, leaf rustle, water, wind) into metallic static. We ended up with three cleanup modes in the manifest: `full` (filters + denoise for impacts), `filter` (80 Hz HP / 11 kHz LP only for broadband textures), and `profile` (denoise learned from a quiet slice of the same clip).
5. **Keep the manifest as the single source of truth, and test on real hardware last.** Having `export` rebuild deterministically from raws meant stray audition takes never leaked into the game. And while an AI listening pass over headless mix captures eliminated \~90% of the tedious mix hunting, phone speakers in a real playthrough still caught things desktop headphones didn't.

Happy to answer questions about the Godot audio setup, the Stable Audio 3 CPU workflow, or the manifest pipeline!
